intro.heading_en: The Boons to Suratha and the Merchant
intro.carita: Uttama Carita (the third episode, chapters 5–13), of which this is the last chapter, and the last chapter of the whole Devī Māhātmya. In the recitation tradition the presiding form of the third carita is Mahāsarasvatī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 5), not a statement of the Purāṇa text. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 13 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna: the auspicious one (शिवा), shining like the disc of the rising sun, four-armed and three-eyed, holding the noose and the goad and showing the gestures of boon and fearlessness (बालार्कमण्डलाभासां … शिवां भजे). The pāṭha also closes the carita with the bīja it opened with: क्लीं stands at the head of chapter 5 and after the last line here (13.29), as ऐं frames chapter 1 and ह्रीं chapters 2–4. The dhyāna and the bījas are liturgy; the chapter itself names none of them.
intro.summary: Medhas ends his account: this is the greatness of the Goddess, by whom the world is upheld (13.2). He gives the answer to the question the king asked in chapter 1: knowledge too is the work of Viṣṇu’s Māyā, and by her the king, the merchant and the discerning are deluded, have been and will be (13.3–4). His counsel is a single imperative: take refuge in her, for, worshipped, she gives enjoyment, heaven and liberation (13.4–5). Mārkaṇḍeya takes up the story again (13.6). Suratha bows to the seer and, sick of his own clinging and of the loss of his kingdom, goes at once to practise austerity with the merchant, on the sandy bank of a river, to see the Mother (13.7–9). There they recite the hymn to the Goddess, make an image of her from the earth of the bank, and worship it with flowers, incense, fire-offerings and water, fasting or eating little, their minds fixed on her; they offer even an oblation sprinkled with their own blood (13.10–12). After three years Caṇḍikā, pleased, appears before them in person and offers each whatever he asks (13.13–15). The king chooses a kingdom that will not be lost in another birth and his own kingdom back in this one; the merchant, turned from the world, chooses the knowledge that frees from ‘mine’ and ‘I’ (13.16–18). The Goddess grants both: in a few days the king will regain his kingdom and rule unshaken, and after death, born of the Sun-god Vivasvat, he will be the Manu called Sāvarṇi; the merchant will have knowledge, for his final fulfilment (13.19–25). She vanishes as they praise her, and Mārkaṇḍeya closes with the promise of 1.2–3 kept: Suratha will be born of the Sun and become Sāvarṇi, the Manu (13.26–29).
intro.forms: The Goddess by whom the world is upheld (यया इदं धार्यते जगत्, 13.2); the Māyā of the Lord Viṣṇu that works both delusion and knowledge (भगवद्विष्णुमाया, 13.3); the supreme Sovereign in whom one takes refuge (परमेश्वरी, 13.4); the giver of enjoyment, heaven and release (भोगस्वर्गापवर्गदा, 13.5); the Mother whom the two men go to see (अम्बा, 13.9); an image of clay on a river bank (मूर्तिः महीमयी, 13.10); and Caṇḍikā, mother and sustainer of the world, who appears in person (जगद्धात्री … चण्डिका, 13.13) and speaks her last words in the text (13.15, 13.20–25). The pāṭha’s dhyāna adds the form of the rising sun with noose, goad, boon and fearlessness.
intro.significance: The chapter closes two stories at once. Medhas’s teaching, begun when the king asked why a man who knows better still clings (1.40–45), ends in counsel, not in argument: take refuge (13.4). And Mārkaṇḍeya’s frame, begun with the promise to tell how Sāvarṇi became the eighth Manu (1.2–3), ends with that promise kept (13.22–23, 13.29). Between the two lies the step the earlier chapters only describe: here the human hearers of the three stories worship for themselves, and the Goddess, who has so far appeared to gods and fought demons, appears to a king and a merchant and grants what each asks. The two requests, a kingdom and knowledge, are read in the tradition as the two goals named in 13.5, enjoyment and release.
intro.grammar: A short chapter with a clear grammar of narrative and promise. The perfect carries the story, including duals for the two worshippers (चक्रतुः 13.11, ददतुः 13.12) and the ātmanepada perfects तेपे (13.10) and वव्रे (13.17); a genitive absolute gives the circumstance (समाराधयतोः, 13.12). The Goddess speaks in futures: simple (प्राप्स्यते, भविष्यति, 13.20–25) and, in the last line, periphrastic (भविता, 13.29). Passives recur where the speaker keeps the agent in the background (धार्यते 13.2, क्रियते 13.3, मोह्यन्ते 13.4, प्रार्थ्यते and प्राप्यताम् 13.15). Absolutives link the actions (श्रुत्वा, प्रणिपत्य, हत्वा, सम्प्राप्य, दत्त्वा, लब्ध्वा, समासाद्य); भवान् takes a third-person verb (13.20, 13.23); and the merchant’s request quotes ‘mine’ and ‘I’ with इति (ममेत्यहमिति, 13.18).
intro.teaching: Literally, a sage finishes his story, a king and a merchant worship the Goddess for three years, she appears, and each receives what he asked for: a kingdom now and a Manu’s reign hereafter for the king, knowledge for the merchant. As teaching, the Śākta tradition reads the chapter as the practical end of the whole text: the power that deludes the wise is also the giver of knowledge (13.3), and the way out of delusion is not more argument but refuge in her (13.4). Worship is shown in its fullness, outward rite and inward collection together (13.10–12), and its fruit is direct vision (प्रत्यक्षम्, 13.13). The two boons are read as bhoga and apavarga (13.5); the Goddess grants both without judging either, but the text names precisely what the merchant’s knowledge undoes: the thoughts ‘mine’ and ‘I’ (13.18), the very mamatā Medhas diagnosed in chapter 1. These readings are the tradition’s and the reader’s; the chapter itself tells the story without comment.
themes: Refuge (śaraṇa) as the end of the teaching
Delusion and knowledge from one power
Worship that leads to direct vision
Bhoga and apavarga: the two boons
The frame closed: Suratha becomes Sāvarṇi

conclusion.narrative: The Devī Māhātmya ends where it began. In chapter 1 a king who had lost his kingdom and a merchant thrown out by his family asked why they still clung to what had rejected them, and Medhas answered with a name, Mahāmāyā, and with three stories to show who she is. In the first (chapter 1) she does not fight at all: as Yoganidrā she withdraws from the sleeping Viṣṇu, who wakes and kills Madhu and Kaiṭabha. In the second (chapters 2–4) she takes form from the gods’ own radiance, destroys Mahiṣa and his armies, and when the gods praise her promises to come whenever she is remembered. In the third (chapters 5–13) she comes forth from Pārvatī’s body, destroys Śumbha, Niśumbha and their generals, declares that the many goddesses are herself alone, and, praised as Nārāyaṇī, promises to return whenever the world is oppressed. Chapter 12 names the fruits of hearing these stories. Chapter 13 turns the hearers into worshippers. Medhas’s last word is ‘take refuge’ (13.4); the two men go to a river bank, worship an image of clay for three years, and see the Goddess face to face (13.13). The king asks for his kingdom and receives more than he knew to ask for, a Manu’s age (13.17, 13.20–23); the merchant asks for the knowledge that ends ‘mine’ and ‘I’ and receives it (13.18, 13.25). She vanishes, as she vanished from the gods after the second story (बभूवान्तर्हिता, 4.39 and 13.28), and the last line answers the first promise of the text: Suratha will be born of the Sun and become Sāvarṇi, the Manu (13.29; compare 1.2–3).

constructions: The perfect dual for the two worshippers acting together (चक्रतुः, 13.11; ददतुः, 13.12).
The genitive absolute for a circumstance (एवं समाराधयतोः … यतात्मनोः, ‘while they were worshipping thus’, 13.12), with the main clause in the next line (13.13).
Passives of request and grant: यत् प्रार्थ्यते त्वया … मत्तः तत् प्राप्यताम् (13.15), and the passive of the causative धार्यते (13.2).
Present, past and future side by side: मोह्यन्ते, मोहिताः, मोहम् एष्यन्ति (13.4).
Futures of promise: simple future (प्राप्स्यते, भविष्यति, 13.20–25) and periphrastic future (भविता, 13.29) for an age still to come.
Respectful भवान् with a third-person verb (प्राप्स्यते भवान्, 13.20; मनुः भवान् … भविष्यति, 13.23).
Quoted words closed by इति: मम इति अहम् इति (13.18).
The plural of majesty: मत्तः ‘from me’ (13.15) beside अस्मत्तः ‘from us’ (13.24).
insights: The power that deludes is the power that gives knowledge: Medhas’s last teaching (13.3) restates 1.57–58, so the text ends on the doctrine with which it began.
No one is outside her delusion, not even the discerning, in any time (13.3–4); the remedy offered is not insight but refuge (13.4).
Worship is both outward and inward: flowers, incense, fire and water, and also fasting, a mind fixed on her and collected (13.10–11). Its fruit is to see her (13.9, 13.13).

She gives what is asked, and gives each seeker his own goal: enjoyment to the king, release to the merchant (13.5, 13.17–18, 13.20–25). Medhas had said as much: asked, and pleased, she gives knowledge and prosperity (12.37).
Her gift exceeds the request: the king asks for an imperishable kingdom and is made a Manu, ruler of an age (13.17, 13.22–23).
The knowledge the merchant receives is named exactly: the end of ‘mine’ and ‘I’ (13.18), the mamatā that bound both men in chapter 1 (1.41, 1.53).
conclusion.srividya: The chapter shares names with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): Viṣṇumāyā (339, विष्णुमाया) and Vidyā (549, विद्या) with 13.3; Parameśvarī (396, परमेश्वरी) with 13.4; स्वर्गापवर्गदा (764), ‘giver of heaven and release’, closely parallel to भोगस्वर्गापवर्गदा in 13.5; Caṇḍikā (755, चण्डिका) and Jagaddhātrī (935, जगद्धात्री) with 13.13; and ज्ञानदा (643) and मुक्तिदा (736), giver of knowledge and of liberation, the gifts of 13.25. The pāṭha’s dhyāna for this chapter, the Goddess bright as the rising sun with noose and goad, recalls the Lalitā Sahasranāma’s उद्यद्भानुसहस्राभा (6), रागस्वरूपपाशाढ्या (8) and क्रोधाकाराङ्कुशोज्ज्वला (9); but its other hands show boon and fearlessness, not Lalitā’s sugarcane bow and flower arrows, and the dhyāna is liturgy, not the Purāṇa text. These are shared Śākta names and images, not evidence that one text depends on the other; no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: Medhas closes his account: this is the Devī Māhātmya, and such is the power of the Goddess by whom the world is upheld.
Deluded now, in the past and in the future — take refuge, great king, in her, the supreme Sovereign.
Worshipped, she alone gives men enjoyment, heaven and liberation.
After three years Caṇḍikā, mother of the world, is pleased and appears before them in person.
The merchant chooses the knowledge that frees from the attachment of ‘mine’ and ‘I’.
The Goddess’s promise to the king: you will be the Manu on earth named Sāvarṇi.
The last line of the text: born of the Sun, Suratha will become Sāvarṇi, the Manu — the promise of 1.2–3 kept.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi is the commonest junction: -aḥ before voiced consonants → -o (सद्यो भक्त्या, सावर्णिको नाम), visarga → s/ś before t/c (ददतुस्तौ, यश्च), visarga → r after other vowels (ऋषिरुवाच, मनुर्भवान्, सावर्णिर्भविता), and the special rule for सः and एषः (स नराधिपः, त्वमेष वैश्यश्च).
Vowel sandhi: vṛddhi (तथैव, सैव, अत्रैव, उपैहि), savarṇa-dīrgha (चापरे, बभूवान्तर्हिता), guṇa (ययेदं, ममेत्यहमिति) and yaṇ (अविभ्रंश्यन्यजन्मनि, देव्युवाच).
Consonant sandhi: voicing (जगद्धात्री, देवाद्विवस्वतः), voicing with palatal assimilation (सूर्याज्जन्म), nasal assimilation (तन्मनस्कौ) and ṣṭutva after a prefix (अभिष्टुता).
Anusvāra for final m before consonants throughout (प्रत्यक्षं प्राह, तं प्रयच्छामि).
samasa: Ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas name the text and its persons (देवीमाहात्म्यम्, नराधिपः, जगद्धात्री, कुलनन्दन, क्षत्रियर्षभः).
Bahuvrīhis describe the worshippers (शंसितव्रतम्, निर्विण्णमानसः, and the duals निराहारौ, यताहारौ, तन्मनस्कौ, यतात्मनोः).
An itaretara dvandva lists the gifts and the offerings (भोगस्वर्गापवर्ग, पुष्पधूपाग्नितर्पणैः); the first stands inside the upapada compound भोगस्वर्गापवर्गदा.
Nested tatpuruṣas: निजगात्रासृगुक्षितम्, सङ्गविच्युतिकारकम्, भगवद्विष्णुमायया, नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः.
Nañ tatpuruṣas (अविभ्रंशि, अस्खलितम्) and avyayībhāvas (प्रत्यक्षम्, यथाभिलषितम्).
grammar_notes: प्राप्स्यते (13.20) has an ātmanepada ending on a parasmaipada root, read as a licence of Epic and Purāṇic verse, not as a passive.
तेपे (13.10) is the ātmanepada perfect of √तप् with तपस् as object; वव्रे (13.17) the ātmanepada perfect of √वृ ‘to choose’.
The singulars जगाम and नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः (13.9) and तपस्तेपे (13.10) agree with the nearest subject, though both men act; the dual returns with तौ (13.10).
हत्वा (13.21) has its agent only in the genitive तव, a loose but common Purāṇic construction; the recipient of a gift stands in the genitive (तयोः, 13.27).
संसिद्ध्यै (13.25) is the optional dative in -ऐ of an i-stem, with the dh doubled before y as the Gita Press prints it.
The last line uses the periphrastic future भविता (13.29), the luṭ of a future not of today.

13.29: the digital source repeats 13.28cd–13.29 as a block numbered 30; the repetition is removed on the colophon’s count of 29 mantras (700 in all), and the closing क्लीं ॐ placed after 13.29 (a structural correction in corrections.json, not a variant).

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading itself, are flagged on 13.3 (the terse विद्या तथैव क्रियते), 13.9 (singular नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः; the listener addressed as महामुने), 13.10 (स च वैश्यः: the king and the merchant, or the merchant too) and 13.25 (which clause संसिद्ध्यै goes with); 13.11 carries the variant above.

comm.t: Medhas speaks for the last time to King Suratha and the merchant Samādhi. The Goddess has given her promises at the end of chapter 12; the seer now draws his teaching to a close, and the frame story begun in chapter 1 is completed.

In the Gita Press pāṭha the chapter is preceded by its own dhyāna: the Goddess shining like the disc of the rising sun, four-armed and three-eyed, holding noose, goad and the gestures of boon and fearlessness (बालार्कमण्डलाभासां … शिवां भजे). The dhyāna and the bīja ॐ that opens this mantra in recitation belong to the pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa.

mantras.lit: This supreme greatness of the Goddess has been told to you, O king. Of such power is that Goddess by whom this world is upheld.
mantras.tr: I have told you, O king, this supreme account of the Goddess’s greatness. Such is the power of the Goddess by whom this world is sustained.
mantras.tr_note: The passive कथितम् (‘has been told’) is rendered actively, ‘I have told’, with the understood agent supplied.

comm.t: Medhas closes his narrative. The compound देवीमाहात्म्यम् here names what he has told — the greatness of the Goddess — and it is the name the whole text bears in its colophons (देवीमाहात्म्ये).

The verse joins two of her works: she has shown her power in the three stories, and she sustains (धार्यते) the world. Medhas had said the same in 12.36: she, though eternal, comes forth again and again to protect the world.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is a complete passive sentence. The second line names the subjects of the verbs in 13.4 (तया … मोह्यन्ते): the sentence runs on.
mantras.lit: Knowledge, likewise, is brought about by the Māyā of the blessed Viṣṇu. By her you, this merchant, and likewise other men of discernment —
mantras.tr: And knowledge, too, is wrought by the same Māyā of the Lord Viṣṇu. By her you and this merchant, and other discerning men as well,
mantras.tr_note: The sentence of the second line is completed in 13.4.

comm.t: Medhas returns to the question with which the king began (1.40–45): why do men who know better remain bound? The answer is the one given in chapter 1: Viṣṇu’s Māyā. Here he adds the other side — knowledge too (विद्या) is her work.

The verse restates 1.57–58: she is the supreme knowledge (विद्या परमा), the cause of release, and also the cause of the bondage of saṃsāra. Delusion and knowledge come from one power; that is why the remedy proposed in 13.4 is to take refuge in her.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also calls her Viṣṇumāyā (name 339, विष्णुमाया) and Vidyā (name 549, विद्या). The shared names reflect a common Śākta idea; the texts are separate.

flags.uncertain: विद्या तथैव क्रियते (Gita Press) is terse: ‘knowledge is likewise made by Viṣṇu’s Māyā’. The sense taken here — the power that deludes also grants knowledge — follows Medhas’s own words in 1.57–58; a reading of विद्या as the object of delusion is not supported by the grammar (it is the subject of the passive क्रियते).

mantras.anvaya: (तया त्वम् एषः वैश्यः च अन्ये विवेकिनः) मोह्यन्ते, मोहिताः च एव, अपरे च मोहम् एष्यन्ति। महाराज, तां परमेश्वरीं शरणम् उपैहि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes 13.3: three verbs in three tenses (मोह्यन्ते, मोहिताः, एष्यन्ति). The plural verb includes त्वम् among third-person subjects, a loose agreement common in Purāṇic verse. The second line is an imperative with a predicative accusative (शरणम्).
mantras.lit: — are deluded, and have been deluded, and others will go into delusion. Go, O great king, to her, the supreme Sovereign, as refuge.
mantras.tr: are deluded now; others have been deluded, and others yet will fall into delusion. Take refuge, great king, in her, the supreme Sovereign.
mantras.tr_note: The three tenses are distributed over different people for clarity; the Sanskrit lists the verbs without naming separate subjects for the first two.

comm.t: The teaching ends in counsel. Delusion is universal — present, past and future — and even the discerning are not exempt. The remedy is not argument but refuge: ‘go to her’.

Taking refuge (शरणागति) is the step that leads to the austerities of 13.8–12. The king had asked who Mahāmāyā is (1.60); the answer has filled twelve chapters, and its practical conclusion is this imperative.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has परमेश्वरी as name 396. The title is common to Śākta hymns; nothing more specific is implied.

mantras.lit: She alone, propitiated, is the giver to men of enjoyment, heaven and release.
mantras.tr: Worshipped, she alone grants to men enjoyment, heaven and final liberation.

comm.t: Medhas’s last words. The worship he recommends is not for one goal only: the same Goddess gives worldly enjoyment, heaven and release. The rest of the chapter shows two of these at once — a kingdom for Suratha, knowledge for the merchant.
अपवर्ग is final liberation (mokṣa). The tradition reads the pair of seekers through this verse: one asks for bhoga, the other for apavarga, and both are granted (13.17–25).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the closely parallel name स्वर्गापवर्गदा (name 764), ‘giver of heaven and release’. The phrase is shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.

mantras.lit: — having bowed down to that greatly blessed seer of praiseworthy vows, weary through his excessive sense of ‘mine’ and the seizure of his kingdom —
mantras.tr: bowed low before that illustrious seer, so steadfast in his vows. Sick at heart from his own clinging and from the loss of his kingdom,
mantras.tr_note: The participial phrase is rendered as a separate clause; the sentence still runs on to 13.9.

comm.t: The king bows to his teacher and goes. Two causes of his weariness are named together: the inner one (excessive ममत्व, the sense of ‘mine’) and the outer one (the loss of the kingdom). The first is what the teaching diagnosed (1.41: ममत्वं गतराज्यस्य).
A modern reading: the verse puts the private cause before the public one. Suratha’s grief came less from what he had lost than from how tightly he had held it.

mantras.anvaya: (सुरथः) सद्यः तपसे जगाम, सः वैश्यः च, महामुने। अम्बायाः संदर्शनार्थं नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः (अभवत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main verb जगाम completes the sentence of 13.7–8. Its subject is Suratha; the merchant is added with च. The second line gives the purpose (संदर्शनार्थम्) and the place (नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः).
mantras.lit: — went at once to austerity, and that merchant too, O great sage; for the sake of seeing the Mother, staying on the sandbank of a river.
mantras.tr: he went at once to practise austerity, great sage, and the merchant with him. To behold the Mother, they settled on the sandy bank of a river.
mantras.tr_note: The singular participle नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः is rendered with ‘they’, since both men stay on the river bank (13.10: तौ तस्मिन् पुलिने).

comm.t: The king and the merchant leave at once for austerity. Their purpose is stated plainly: to see the Mother (अम्बा). The vocative महामुने is Mārkaṇḍeya’s address to his own listener — a reminder that the whole story is being told inside the Purāṇa’s frame.
The river bank (पुलिन) is a classic place of tapas: open, quiet and near water for the rites. The Devī Māhātmya does not name the river.

flags.uncertain: नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः is singular although both men stay on the bank; it is read with the nearest subject (or with each). The listener addressed as महामुने is, in the Purāṇa’s frame, Krauṣṭuki (see 1.1).

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete: two subjects with a singular verb and a participle of accompanying action. The second line begins a new sentence whose verb is in 13.11.
mantras.lit: And he and the merchant practised austerity, reciting the supreme Devīsūkta. The two, having made on that sandbank an earthen image of the Goddess —
mantras.tr: There the king and the merchant practised austerities, chanting the supreme hymn to the Goddess. On that sandbank they shaped an image of the Goddess out of clay,
mantras.tr_note: सः ‘he’ is rendered ‘the king’. The sentence of the second line is completed in 13.11.

comm.t: The worship begins: austerity, recitation of a hymn, and an image of the Goddess made from the earth of the river bank. Everything they use is at hand; nothing is bought or brought.

Which hymn is meant by देवीसूक्त is debated in the tradition. One view identifies it with the Vedic Devīsūkta (Ṛgveda 10.125, the hymn of Vāk) recited with the Saptaśatī; another with the hymn of the gods in chapter 5 (5.9 ff., नमो देव्यै महादेव्यै), which the pāṭha tradition also calls a Devīsūkta. The text itself does not say.
A modern reading: the image is made of the same earth on which they sit. The Goddess they seek is worshipped first in the most ordinary material there is.

flags.uncertain: स च वैश्यः is read ‘he (the king) and the merchant’, with the singular verb agreeing with the nearest subject (both men worship in the next line: तौ). It can also be read ‘and that merchant too (practised austerity)’, the king’s austerity being already stated in 13.9; the meaning of the scene is the same.

mantras.anvaya: (तौ, 13.10) निराहारौ यताहारौ तन्मनस्कौ समाहितौ (सन्तौ) पुष्पधूपाग्नितर्पणैः तस्याः अर्हणां चक्रतुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main verb चक्रतुः completes the sentence begun in 13.10 (तौ … कृत्वा). The four duals of the second line describe the two worshippers.
mantras.lit: — performed her worship with flowers, incense, fire and libations, fasting, restrained in food, their minds on her, concentrated.
mantras.tr: and worshipped her with flowers, incense, fire-offerings and libations of water — fasting, or eating little, their minds on her alone, wholly collected.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Fire-offerings’ and ‘libations of water’ interpret अग्नि and तर्पण as rites. ‘Fasting, or eating little’ renders the pair निराहारौ यताहारौ as alternating disciplines; the Sanskrit simply sets the two words side by side.

comm.t: The worship of the earthen image is complete in its forms: flowers, incense, oblations in fire and libations of water. The four duals of the second line describe the inner discipline that goes with the outer rite: food withheld or restrained, the mind fixed on her, collected.

Variant: for निराहारौ यताहारौ (Gita Press, kept here) GRETIL and Freund read निराहारौ यतात्मानौ, ‘fasting, self-controlled’. The Gita Press pair can be understood as successive or alternating stages of the vow — at times no food, at times measured food; the other reading removes the apparent tension. The word यतात्मनोः in 13.12 is common to both.

mantras.anvaya: तौ निजगात्रासृगुक्षितं बलिं च एव ददतुः। एवं त्रिभिः वर्षैः समाराधयतोः यतात्मनोः (तयोः, 13.13: … चण्डिका प्राह)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete. The second line is a genitive absolute (समाराधयतोः … यतात्मनोः) on which the main clause of 13.13 depends.
mantras.lit: And they two also gave an offering sprinkled with the blood of their own limbs. While the two self-controlled ones were thus worshipping, in three years —
mantras.tr: They offered, too, an oblation moistened with blood from their own bodies. When they had worshipped thus with self-restraint for three years,
mantras.tr_note: The genitive absolute is rendered as a ‘when’ clause; the instrumental त्रिभिः वर्षैः (‘in three years’) is rendered ‘for three years’.

comm.t: The worship reaches its height: an offering (बलि) sprinkled with the worshippers’ own blood. The text states it without comment; it marks how far their devotion went. Three years of such worship pass before the Goddess appears.

The offering is of themselves, not of another life: the vow costs the worshippers their own blood. Their wholeness of intent (यतात्मनोः, ‘self-controlled’) is what the verse stresses as the condition of the Goddess’s appearing in the next line.
A modern reading: what is offered is the body that had served attachment. Their worship spends what they had spent their lives protecting.

mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause on which the genitive absolute of 13.12 depends.
mantras.lit: — Caṇḍikā, the upholder of the world, fully pleased, spoke in visible form.
mantras.tr: Caṇḍikā, mother and sustainer of the world, well pleased, appeared before them and spoke.
mantras.tr_note: प्रत्यक्षम् (‘visibly’) is rendered ‘appeared before them and’; ‘mother and sustainer’ renders धात्री, which means both nurse and upholder.

comm.t: The end of the austerity: after three years the Goddess, pleased, speaks to them directly, in visible form. The purpose stated in 13.9 — to see the Mother — is fulfilled.
प्रत्यक्षम् is the point of the verse: the Goddess who has been known through the seer’s narration is now seen by the hearers themselves. Teaching leads to worship, and worship to direct vision.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has both names: जगद्धात्री (name 935) and चण्डिका (name 755). Shared epithets of Śākta devotion; the texts are separate.

mantras.anvaya: भूप, यत् त्वया प्रार्थ्यते, कुलनन्दन, (यत्) त्वया च (प्रार्थ्यते), तत् सर्वं मत्तः प्राप्यताम्। परितुष्टा (अहम्) तत् ददामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative–correlative sentence (यत् … तत्) in the passive, with two agents each addressed by name; then a short active sentence in the first person.
mantras.lit: Whatever is asked for by you, O king, and by you, O joy of your family — let all that be obtained from me. Fully pleased, I give it.
mantras.tr: Whatever you ask, O king, and you, joy of your house — receive it all from me. I am well pleased; I grant it.
mantras.tr_note: The passives (‘is asked for’, ‘let it be obtained’) are rendered actively.

comm.t: The Goddess offers each of them a boon, addressing them one at a time: the king (भूप) and the merchant (कुलनन्दन). Her offer is unlimited — whatever they ask.

कुलनन्दन, ‘joy of your family’, is a courteous address; but the merchant’s own family had driven him out for his wealth (1.22–23). The title may be read as conventional, or as the Goddess restoring to him the honour his kin denied him.

mantras.anvaya: ततः नृपः अन्यजन्मनि अविभ्रंशि राज्यम्, अत्र एव च बलात् हतशत्रुबलं निजं राज्यं वव्रे।
mantras.anvaya_en: One verb (वव्रे) with two objects, each a kingdom: one ‘in another birth’, one ‘here itself’, joined by च.
mantras.lit: Then the king chose an imperishable kingdom in another birth, and here itself his own kingdom, its enemies’ forces destroyed by force.
mantras.tr: Then the king chose a kingdom that would never be lost, in another life — and, in this very life, his own kingdom back, his enemies’ power broken by force.

comm.t: The king’s choice is double: a lasting sovereignty in a future birth, and the return of his own kingdom now. Both are worldly; he asks for the restoration of what was lost and for more than he had.

Suratha’s request is read as the choice of bhoga, enjoyment — the first of the gifts Medhas named in 13.5 (भोगस्वर्गापवर्गदा). The Goddess grants it without reproach; the text does not judge the choice.

mantras.anvaya: ततः निर्विण्णमानसः प्राज्ञः सः वैश्यः अपि ‘मम’ इति ‘अहम्’ इति सङ्गविच्युतिकारकं ज्ञानं वव्रे।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject with three qualifiers, verb and object. The quoted words ‘मम’ इति ‘अहम्’ इति define the attachment (सङ्ग) that the knowledge removes.
mantras.lit: That merchant too, then, his mind disenchanted, the wise one, chose knowledge that brings about the falling-away of attachment (expressed as) ‘mine’ and ‘I’.
mantras.tr: The merchant, his heart turned from the world, wisely chose knowledge — the knowledge that frees one from the attachment of ‘mine’ and ‘I’.
mantras.tr_note: The epithet प्राज्ञः (‘the wise one’) is rendered adverbially (‘wisely’).

comm.t: The merchant chooses the other gift: knowledge that releases attachment. The text names that attachment precisely — the thoughts ‘mine’ and ‘I’. It was this that had kept both men bound to people and things they knew had wronged them (1.41–45).

The tradition reads the merchant’s choice as apavarga, liberation — the last of the gifts in 13.5. The two men, who came to the seer with the same affliction, leave with the two great goals: enjoyment and release.
A modern reading: the merchant had more reason than the king to ask for his property back. He asks instead to be free of needing it.

mantras.anvaya: भूयः च मृतः (भवान्) विवस्वतः देवात् जन्म सम्प्राप्य (13.23: … मनुः भविष्यति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A participle and an absolutive phrase describing the subject भवान् of 13.23, where the sentence ends.
mantras.lit: And, having died, having again obtained birth from the god Vivasvat —
mantras.tr: And when you have died, you will be born again of the Sun-god Vivasvat,
mantras.tr_note: The participle and absolutive are rendered as finite clauses; the sentence ends in 13.23. भूयः ‘again’ is taken with सम्प्राप्य जन्म (‘born again’).

comm.t: The second part of the king’s boon looks beyond this life: after death he will be born of the Sun-god Vivasvat. This is the ‘imperishable kingdom in another birth’ he asked for (13.17).
The verse ties the end of the text to its beginning: 1.2 introduced Sāvarṇi as ‘the son of the Sun’ (सूर्यतनयः), and 1.3 as ‘son of Ravi’. The king of the story is now revealed as that future Manu.

morph.note: A taddhita derivative in -इक from सावर्णि, ‘belonging to / descended from Sāvarṇi’. The Purāṇa uses सावर्णिक of the age (सावर्णिके मन्वन्तरे in every colophon) and here of the Manu himself; 13.29 has the simple name सावर्णिः.
Locative of the monosyllabic ū-stem भू ‘earth’: ū becomes uv before a vowel ending (भुव् + इ).
Simple future of √भू: guṇa (भो → भव्) + -इष्य- + -ति. With a predicate nominative, ‘will become’.

mantras.anvaya: (मृतः विवस्वतः जन्म सम्प्राप्य, 13.22) भवान् भुवि सावर्णिकः नाम मनुः भविष्यति।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause of 13.22–23: subject भवान्, predicate सावर्णिकः नाम मनुः, verb भविष्यति.
mantras.lit: — you will be on earth the Manu named Sāvarṇika.
mantras.tr: and you will be the Manu on earth, named Sāvarṇi.
mantras.tr_note: सावर्णिकः is rendered by the name the text uses at its beginning and end, Sāvarṇi (1.2, 13.29).

comm.t: The promise in full: the king will be a Manu, the father and ruler of a whole age of mankind. The question with which Mārkaṇḍeya began (1.2: how Sāvarṇi became the eighth Manu) is answered in the Goddess’s own words.
The ‘imperishable kingdom’ of 13.17 is a manvantara: a sovereignty larger and longer than any earthly reign. The Goddess grants more than the king knew how to ask for.

mantras.anvaya: वैश्यवर्य, त्वया च अस्मत्तः यः वरः अभिवाञ्छितः, (13.25: तं प्रयच्छामि …)।

mantras.lit: And, O best of merchants, the boon which has been desired by you from us —
mantras.tr: And you, best of merchants — the boon you have sought from me,
mantras.tr_note: The plural of majesty अस्मत्तः is rendered ‘from me’; the passive is rendered actively.

comm.t: The Goddess turns to the merchant. She speaks of herself in the plural of majesty (अस्मत्तः), which she did not use when offering the boons (मत्तः, 13.15).

morph.note: Present of प्र + √दा. For the bhvādi root दा (दाण्) Pāṇini substitutes यच्छ- in the present system (as गच्छ- for √गम्); प्रयच्छति ‘offers, grants’ is the common form.
Dative of the feminine i-stem संसिद्धि with the optional ending -ऐ (संसिद्ध्यै beside संसिद्धये). The Gita Press doubles the dh before y, as in युद्ध्यसे (10.3).
With the genitive तव, ‘will be yours’ — the usual Sanskrit way of saying ‘you will have’.

mantras.anvaya: तं प्रयच्छामि। संसिद्ध्यै तव ज्ञानं भविष्यति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two short sentences: the grant (तं प्रयच्छामि, completing 13.24) and its content (ज्ञानं भविष्यति), with संसिद्ध्यै giving the purpose.
mantras.lit: — that I grant. For complete perfection, knowledge will be yours.
mantras.tr: I grant it. You shall have knowledge, for your final fulfilment.

comm.t: The second boon is granted in a few words: the merchant will have knowledge, and its purpose is संसिद्धि, complete attainment. What knowledge he asked for was stated in 13.18 — the knowledge that ends ‘mine’ and ‘I’.

संसिद्धि is read in the tradition as final liberation (mokṣa), matching the merchant’s request; the king receives the reward of bhoga, the merchant that of apavarga (13.5). Medhas had foretold both in 12.37: when asked, and pleased, she gives knowledge (विज्ञानम्) and prosperity (ऋद्धिम्).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names her ज्ञानदा, ‘giver of knowledge’ (name 643), and मुक्तिदा, ‘giver of liberation’ (name 736). The same two gifts; the texts are separate.

flags.uncertain: संसिद्ध्यै can be taken with either clause: ‘I grant it for (your) perfection’ or ‘for perfection, knowledge will be yours’. The meaning is the same; the second is followed in the anvaya.

comm.t: The last speaker label of the text. Mārkaṇḍeya closes the story in his own voice: the Goddess vanishes, and the frame returns to Sāvarṇi, with whom it began (1.2).

mantras.tr: Having granted each of them the boon he desired, the Goddess
mantras.tr_note: The sentence is completed in the first line of 13.28.

comm.t: Both boons have been given, each exactly as asked (यथाभिलषितम्). The Goddess grants what the worshipper wants, without correcting his request.

samasa.alt: Also an upamita karmadhāraya, क्षत्रियः ऋषभः इव (‘a warrior like a bull’), the analysis grammarians give for compounds of ‘tiger’, ‘bull’ and the like; the sense ‘chief of warriors’ is the same.

morph.note: अन्तर् + √धा ‘to put between, hide’: past participle अन्तर्हित (धा → हि before -त). अन्तर् behaves like a verbal prefix and is kept on the participle. With बभूव: ‘became hidden’, i.e. vanished.
अभि + √स्तु: after the i of the prefix the s of the root becomes ṣ, and the following t becomes ṭ beside it (ष्टुना ष्टुः, 8.4.41): अभिष्टुत.
Absolutive of √लभ्: bh + t → bdh (the t is voiced and aspirated after the aspirate, and the bh loses its aspiration): लब्ध्वा.

mantras.anvaya: (13.27: इति तयोः यथाभिलषितं वरं दत्त्वा) ताभ्यां भक्त्या अभिष्टुता देवी सद्यः अन्तर्हिता बभूव। एवं देव्याः वरं लब्ध्वा क्षत्रियर्षभः सुरथः (13.29: … सावर्णिः मनुः भविता)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence of 13.27 (main verb बभूव with the predicate अन्तर्हिता). The second line begins the closing sentence: an absolutive phrase and the subject, whose verb भविता is in 13.29.
mantras.lit: — became vanished at once, praised with devotion by the two. Thus having received the boon from the Goddess, Suratha, the bull among kṣatriyas —
mantras.tr: vanished at once, as the two praised her with devotion. So Suratha, foremost of warriors, having received the Goddess’s boon,
mantras.tr_note: The participle अभिष्टुता is rendered as a clause (‘as the two praised her’). The second line runs on to 13.29.

comm.t: The Goddess disappears at once, as she did after her promises to the gods (12.33: तत्रैवान्तरधीयत). The last thing the two men do is praise her. The second line turns to the outcome for the king.

Textual note: in the digital source this line and 13.29 are repeated as a further block numbered 30. The chapter’s own colophon counts 29 mantras (uvāca 6, half-ślokas 11, ślokas 12; 700 in all), so the repetition is removed in this edition and the closing bījas are placed after 13.29 (see corrections.json).

morph.note: Periphrastic future (luṭ): agent noun भवितृ in the nominative, standing for the third person singular. Pāṇini assigns luṭ to a future not of today — fitting for a birth in an age still to come.
Absolutive of the causative आसादय- (आ + √सद्, ‘to cause to sit near’, i.e. to reach, obtain) with सम्: the -अय- of the causative is dropped before -य.

mantras.anvaya: (एवं देव्याः वरं लब्ध्वा क्षत्रियर्षभः सुरथः, 13.28) सूर्यात् जन्म समासाद्य सावर्णिः मनुः भविता।
mantras.anvaya_en: The end of the sentence begun in 13.28b: a second absolutive (समासाद्य) and the main verb भविता with its predicate सावर्णिः मनुः.
mantras.lit: — having obtained birth from the Sun, will become Sāvarṇi, the Manu.
mantras.tr: will be born of the Sun and become Sāvarṇi, the Manu.
mantras.tr_note: The absolutive समासाद्य is rendered as a coordinate verb (‘will be born … and become’).

comm.t: The last line of the Devī Māhātmya returns to its first subject. Mārkaṇḍeya had promised to tell how Sāvarṇi, son of the Sun, became the eighth Manu (1.2–3); the answer is this story — a king who lost everything, took refuge in the Goddess, and will be born of the Sun as Sāvarṇi.

In the Gita Press pāṭha the mantra is followed by the bījas क्लीं ॐ, which close the recitation and belong to the pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa. The colophon then names the chapter ‘the granting of boons to Suratha and the merchant’ (सुरथवैश्ययोर्वरप्रदानम्) and completes the count of seven hundred.
A modern reading: the text ends not with the Goddess but with a human future. Its last verb is ‘will be’ (भविता) — the story of her power closes as a promise about what a person will become.
